title: Für Elise
note: Published only in 1867, forty years after Beethoven died. Who “Elise” was is still argued about.

title: “Moonlight” Sonata, first movement
work: Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor, Op. 27 No. 2
note: Beethoven called it “Sonata quasi una fantasia.” The moonlight nickname came later, from the critic Ludwig Rellstab.

title: “Pathétique” Sonata, Adagio cantabile
work: Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, Op. 13, second movement
note: Unlike most of his nicknamed sonatas, Beethoven approved the title “Pathétique” himself.

title: “Pathétique” Sonata, Rondo
work: Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, Op. 13, third movement
note: A rondo: the opening theme keeps returning between contrasting episodes.

title: In the Hall of the Mountain King
work: Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, Op. 46 No. 4
note: Grieg himself grumbled that it reeked of “cow pies” and trollish self-satisfaction.

title: Waltz in A♭
note: Written for piano duet and dedicated to the critic Eduard Hanslick. Brahms later made solo versions.

title: Impromptu in G♭
note: Its first publisher transposed it to G major to make it easier to read.

title: The Entertainer
note: Joplin marked it “Not fast.” The 1973 film The Sting brought it back to everyone’s ears.

title: Maple Leaf Rag
note: Named for the Maple Leaf Club in Sedalia, Missouri. It made Joplin’s name.

title: Elite Syncopations
note: Published by John Stark, who issued many of Joplin’s best-known rags.

title: Solace
note: A habanera rather than a rag. It is marked “Very slow march time.”

title: Bethena
note: A ragtime waltz that moves through several keys.

title: Peacherine Rag

title: Pineapple Rag

title: Sun Flower Slow Drag
note: Written with his student Scott Hayden. A “slow drag” is a dance, taken unhurried.

title: Wall Street Rag
note: Its sections carry captions such as “Panic in Wall Street.” Joplin printed: “It is never right to play Ragtime fast.”

title: Original Rags
note: Joplin’s first published rag, appearing a few months before the Maple Leaf.

title: Magnetic Rag
note: The last rag Joplin published in his lifetime.

title: Amazing Grace
note: Newton was a former slave-ship captain who became an Anglican priest.

title: Holy, Holy, Holy
note: The tune is named after the Council of Nicaea, which defined the doctrine of the Trinity.

title: It Is Well with My Soul
work: Tune VILLE DU HAVRE · Words: Horatio Spafford
note: Spafford wrote the words after his four daughters died in a shipwreck in 1873.

title: Be Thou My Vision
work: Words: ancient Irish, tr. Mary Byrne and Eleanor Hull
note: Slane is the hill where St. Patrick is said to have lit a paschal fire.

title: Abide with Me
work: Tune EVENTIDE · Words: Henry F. Lyte
note: Lyte wrote the words in 1847 as he was dying of tuberculosis.

title: Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing
note: Robinson wrote the text in his early twenties.

title: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
note: Luther wrote both words and tune. Bach later built a cantata on it.

title: Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee
work: Tune HYMN TO JOY · Words: Henry van Dyke, 1907
note: The melody is the “Ode to Joy” from Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony.

title: Blessed Assurance
note: Knapp played the tune for Crosby, who said it sounded like “Blessed assurance, Jesus is mine.”

title: How Firm a Foundation
work: From Joseph Funk’s Genuine Church Music
note: A shape-note tune from the Shenandoah Valley.

title: All Creatures of Our God and King
work: Words: St. Francis of Assisi · harm. Ralph Vaughan Williams, 1906
note: The words come from St. Francis’s “Canticle of the Sun.”

title: Crown Him with Many Crowns
note: Diademata is Greek for “crowns.”

title: What a Friend We Have in Jesus
note: Scriven first wrote the words as a poem to comfort his mother in Ireland.

title: Rock of Ages
note: The tune is named after the author of the words.

title: Praise to the Lord, the Almighty
work: Words: Joachim Neander, tr. Catherine Winkworth
note: The Neander Valley, where Neanderthal remains were found, is named after this hymn writer.

title: The Old Rugged Cross
note: First sung at revival meetings in Michigan.

title: Nearer, My God, to Thee
work: Tune BETHANY · Words: Sarah Flower Adams
note: Some Titanic survivors recalled the ship’s band playing it.

title: Be Still, My Soul
note: The melody comes from Sibelius’s tone poem Finlandia.

title: When I Survey the Wondrous Cross
note: Mason based the tune on a Gregorian chant.

title: Praise God, from Whom All Blessings Flow
work: Tune OLD HUNDREDTH · Words: Thomas Ken
note: This is the tune in its original lively Genevan rhythm.

title: I Need Thee Every Hour
note: Lowry added the refrain to Hawks’s poem.

title: Fairest Lord Jesus
work: Tune ST. ELIZABETH · harm. Richard S. Willis
note: Also sung as “Beautiful Savior.” Sometimes called the Crusaders’ Hymn.

title: Silent Night
work: Tune STILLE NACHT · Words: Joseph Mohr
note: First sung in Oberndorf, Austria, accompanied by guitar.

title: Joy to the World
note: Mason pieced the tune together from echoes of Handel’s Messiah.

title: O Come, All Ye Faithful
note: Originally a Latin hymn, “Adeste fideles.”

title: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded
work: PASSION CHORALE · harm. J. S. Bach
note: Hassler first wrote the melody for a love song. Bach used it five times in the St. Matthew Passion.

title: Savior, Like a Shepherd Lead Us
note: Bradbury also wrote the tune for “Jesus Loves Me.”

title: For the Beauty of the Earth
work: Tune DIX · Words: Folliott S. Pierpoint
note: The tune is named after William Chatterton Dix, who wrote “As with Gladness.”

title: O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing
note: Charles Wesley wrote the text for the first anniversary of his conversion.

title: Immortal, Invisible, God Only Wise
note: The tune began as a Welsh folk song.
